title: Global Markets Weekly Recap & Outlook: November 16–20, 2026
intro: Global financial markets concluded the week of November 16–20, 2026, with broadly mixed performances as persistent inflationary pressures, hawkish monetary policy expectations and renewed geopolitical uncertainty continued to shape investor behaviour across asset classes. The US dollar extended its advance, Treasury yields remained elevated, gold struggled to regain momentum and crude oil posted a second consecutive weekly decline despite intensifying tensions between Washington and Tehran. Equity markets managed to register positive weekly returns overall, though Friday's sharp selloff in semiconductor stocks underscored the fragility of market confidence ahead of Nvidia's highly anticipated quarterly earnings report.

sections.heading: Asset Class Review: Dollar Strength, Gold Headwinds and Oil's Geopolitical Balancing Act
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index climbed above 103 on Friday, reaching its highest level since March 2025, underpinned by persistent inflation data and increasingly hawkish Federal Reserve expectations. October producer prices rose 0.3% month over month, modestly below the 0.4% consensus estimate, yet annual PPI accelerated to 6.5% — its highest reading since November 2022. Core PPI maintained an annual rate of 5.0%, the most elevated since early 2023. Combined with stronger-than-expected consumer inflation and resilient labour market conditions, the data reinforced market pricing for a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, with the possibility of a larger adjustment remaining on the table.

Gold traded relatively unchanged around $3,880 per ounce, unable to attract fresh buying interest in the face of dollar strength and rising Treasury yields, which elevated the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets. Persistent inflation expectations and higher energy prices further complicated the precious metals outlook. While geopolitical uncertainty continued to provide residual support, the dominant macro framework — higher rates, stronger dollar — maintained a cautious bias for gold.

WTI crude traded above $88 per barrel on Friday following a deterioration in US-Iran diplomatic relations. President Trump signalled that Washington may abandon negotiations with Tehran, while Iran insisted that the naval blockade and sanctions regime must be lifted before direct talks could resume. Despite this escalation, crude remained on track for a second consecutive weekly decline as Middle Eastern exports continued to recover, with improving supply conditions offsetting a meaningful portion of the geopolitical risk premium. The market remains structurally caught between disruption risk and gradual supply normalisation.

sections.heading: US Equities: AI Trade Under Scrutiny as Semiconductor Stocks Retreat
sections.content:
Wall Street closed Friday's session on a mixed note, with renewed selling pressure across the semiconductor complex weighing heavily on technology-sensitive indices. The S&P 500 declined 0.4% and the Nasdaq Composite shed 1.2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average managed a modest gain of 51 points. Within the semiconductor space, AMD fell 8.7%, Broadcom declined 4.9%, Nvidia dropped 2.0% and Micron lost 2.5%. Cisco underperformed with a 6.2% decline despite raising its FY2027 guidance, and Applied Materials fell 2.8% notwithstanding record revenues — a signal that elevated expectations are increasingly difficult to satisfy.

Regulatory scrutiny surrounding semiconductor exports to China and growing uncertainty over the sustainability of AI-related capital expenditure amplified the cautious tone. Despite Friday's weakness, weekly performance remained constructive: the S&P 500 gained 1.4%, the Nasdaq 100 advanced 2.1% and the Dow Jones added 472 points. The defining question for the week ahead is whether Nvidia's quarterly results will confirm that the recent semiconductor correction represents a temporary consolidation or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of AI-related valuations.

sections.heading: Weekly Outlook: Key Catalysts and Directional Scenarios
sections.content:
The coming week presents a dense macro and corporate calendar that is likely to be decisive for near-term market direction across all major asset classes.

In the United States, Nvidia's quarterly results on Tuesday represent the single most important corporate event of the week. Investors will scrutinise revenue growth trajectories, forward guidance, AI infrastructure demand and the geopolitical dimension of semiconductor exports. Additional earnings releases include Walmart, Home Depot, Palo Alto Networks, Walt Disney and Intuit. On Wednesday, the FOMC minutes will provide institutional-level insight into policymakers' deliberations — particularly the two dissenting votes favouring an immediate rate increase — and are expected to reinforce or challenge the December tightening consensus. Key US data releases include October Retail Sales (forecast flat, following September's 0.8% gain), Industrial Production (expected +0.1% versus prior +0.7%), Housing Starts (annualised 1.23 million), Building Permits, Pending Home Sales, regional manufacturing surveys and the final November University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment reading.

In the United Kingdom, markets will closely monitor the Consumer Price Index, unemployment and employment data, Retail Sales and Public-Sector Finances. Following Bank of England warnings that inflation could approach 5% by mid-2027, December rate hike expectations have risen materially. In the Eurozone, the focus shifts to German ZEW Economic Sentiment, Euro Area Consumer Confidence and industrial production — the latter expected to rebound following three consecutive monthly contractions. Switzerland will publish Q3 GDP alongside trade and industrial production data.

In Asia-Pacific, China will release a comprehensive data package covering Industrial Production, Retail Sales, Fixed Asset Investment, the House Price Index and the Unemployment Rate. The People's Bank of China is widely expected to hold its one-year and five-year Loan Prime Rates unchanged at 3.0% and 3.5% respectively. Major corporate earnings from Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu and JD will add a significant bottom-up dimension to the regional outlook. In Japan, Q3 GDP is forecast to slow materially to 0.1% quarter over quarter from 0.4% previously, with annualised growth projected at 0.3% — a potential headwind for Japanese equities and regional risk appetite.

sections.heading: Three Macro Themes Defining Market Direction
sections.content:
Three structural forces are expected to dominate market dynamics in the week ahead.

First, the monetary tightening and inflation risk nexus remains the primary macroeconomic driver globally. Elevated annual PPI and CPI readings, combined with labour market resilience, are consolidating expectations for further Federal Reserve action. The US dollar and Treasury yields will remain acutely sensitive to incoming data and Fed communication, maintaining upward pressure on funding costs and risk asset valuations.

Second, AI valuations and Nvidia's earnings present the most consequential single event for equity markets. The recent correction in semiconductor stocks has created a binary setup: strong results and constructive guidance could restore institutional confidence in the AI investment cycle, while a disappointment on revenues or forward outlook risks triggering sustained profit-taking across the technology sector and beyond.

Third, Middle East geopolitics and energy market dynamics continue to introduce non-linear risk. The breakdown in US-Iran diplomacy sustains a geopolitical premium in crude, yet recovering regional supply and improving export flows are exerting countervailing downward pressure. The critical variable is whether geopolitical developments escalate sufficiently to generate a durable supply shock, or whether market fundamentals reassert dominance.

conclusion: The overall market bias for the week of November 16–20 remains cautious. A stronger US dollar, structurally elevated inflation expectations and policy uncertainty collectively create a challenging environment for risk assets across geographies. Equity markets face a critical test from Nvidia's earnings — an event with the potential to either validate or meaningfully reprice the AI-driven growth narrative that has anchored technology valuations through 2026. Gold remains structurally exposed to rising yields and dollar strength, with limited near-term catalysts for a sustained recovery. Crude oil continues to navigate the tension between geopolitical disruption risk and improving supply conditions. The central question for institutional investors is straightforward: can the combination of corporate earnings and economic data sustain current market valuations under a tightening monetary regime, or will persistent inflation expectations force another round of risk reduction across global portfolios?
